analysis.one_liner: Approves the Keystone XL pipeline by deeming every required federal permit already issued.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 241-175 on May 22, 2013, but it never came to a vote in the Senate and died when that Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have approved the Keystone XL oil pipeline from Canada by legislative fiat. Instead of waiting for the State Department's presidential permit and normal agency reviews, it declares that no presidential permit is needed, deems the environmental impact statement complete, and treats every other federal permit - wildlife, water, land right-of-way - as already granted. It also strips the EPA of any power to restrict the project and sends all court challenges to a single friendly-court route with a 60-day filing deadline.
analysis.who_benefits: TransCanada Keystone Pipeline, the company behind the project, gains the most: it gets construction approval without any further permit decisions by federal agencies. Canadian oil sands producers gain a route to Gulf Coast refineries. Pipeline construction contractors would get work and jobs during the build, which the bill's own findings emphasize.

how_it_helps.text: Declares that no presidential permit is required for Keystone XL and treats the 2011 environmental impact statement as satisfying all National Environmental Policy Act and National Historic Preservation Act requirements.

Deems federal permits for endangered-species, land right-of-way, migratory bird, and navigable-waters approvals already issued, and requires the Army Secretary to issue water permits within 90 days - with the permit deemed issued automatically on day 91 if the Secretary has not acted.
Bars the EPA Administrator from prohibiting or restricting any activity the bill authorizes, and lets the Army Secretary waive any procedural requirement he considers desirable.
Channels all legal challenges to the D.C. Court of Appeals with exclusive jurisdiction and a 60-day filing window, on an expedited schedule.
The bill's own findings cite State Department analysis of construction employment and government revenue, and describe pipeline transport of oil as the safest means.

analysis.who_pays: Communities and landowners along the pipeline route bear the spill and water-contamination risk while the safeguards that would normally apply are legislated out of the way. The American burying beetle loses Endangered Species Act protection for takings by the project, and taxpayers could absorb oil-spill costs that the bill, as passed, declined to cover by treating tar-sands material as taxable crude under the Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund - the Democrats' motion to recommit would have required that and was rejected.
analysis.who_pays_short: Communities and waters along the route

drawbacks.text: The bill deems the environmental review complete by law rather than letting agencies finish it, and forbids the EPA from restricting anything the bill authorizes.
It waives Endangered Species Act protection for the American burying beetle and deems federal wildlife and water permits issued without agency decisions.
It funnels all litigation to the D.C. Court of Appeals with a 60-day filing deadline, sharply limiting the ability of landowners or affected communities to contest the project.

The House rejected a motion to recommit that would have required tar-sands material shipped through the pipeline to be taxed as crude oil for the Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund, leaving spill-fund coverage for that material in doubt.

Its supporters' honest case - construction jobs and reduced reliance on other foreign oil - is modest and short-lived, and the bill's own cited State Department finding says approval is unlikely to change the pace of oil-sands development.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The concrete public benefits - temporary construction jobs and a marginal change in oil supply - are small and, by the bill's own findings, unlikely to alter oil-sands output. What the bill actually does is delete a decade of permitting and environmental review for one company's pipeline, shield it from the EPA, and shorten the court window to 60 days. The design is one-sided: nearly all the certainty goes to the company, and nearly all the risk stays with the land and water along the route.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 241-175 in May 2013, but after the Senate received it and put it on its calendar it never came up for a vote, and it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Three House committees reported the bill in May 2013, and the Rules Committee set up floor consideration with 90 minutes of debate under a rule that allowed only specified amendments.
Eight Democratic amendments were debated on the floor and all failed; the House instead adopted the committee's amendment in the nature of a substitute.

A Democratic motion to recommit - to require tar-sands material to be treated as crude oil for the Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund - failed 194-223, with all 201 Democrats voting for it and all Republicans voting no.
The bill passed the House on a recorded vote of 241-175 with 1 present: 222 of 232 Republicans voted yes, while 175 of 201 Democrats voted no and 19 Democrats joined them.
The Senate received the bill on May 23, 2013, read it twice, and placed it on the Legislative Calendar on June 3; no further Senate action was taken before the 113th Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Communities and water resources along the pipeline route are better off, since the bill's stripped-down protections and single-court litigation channel never took effect. The Obama administration kept its authority over the presidential permit, and TransCanada gained nothing from this Congress. The company later pursued the project in other ways, but as of the end of the 113th Congress this route to approval was closed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Communities along the route, not TransCanada

for.name: Rep. Lee Terry
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on March 15, 2013 and shepherded it through committee and floor consideration.

for.name: 132 of 232 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; only 2 House Democrats did.

for.name: Speaker John Boehner
for.what_they_did: Brought the bill to the floor under a rule (H. Res. 228) providing for same-day debate and limiting amendments to a specified list.

for.name: 222 of 232 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Voted yes on passage; not a single Republican voted no.

against.name: 175 of 201 House Democrats
against.what_they_did: Voted no on final passage; also all voted for the motion to recommit requiring tar-sands material to be taxed for the Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund.

against.name: Sen. Harry Reid
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a Senate vote after it was placed on the calendar in June 2013.

against.name: President Barack Obama
against.what_they_did: Opposed congressional attempts to approve Keystone XL and preserve his administration's authority over the presidential permit, including veto threats against such legislation.

against.name: Rep. Tim Bishop
against.what_they_did: Moved to recommit with instructions to require tar-sands material shipped through the pipeline to be taxed as crude for the Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund.

sides.party_line_note: The final vote split almost entirely by party: 222 of 232 Republicans voted yes with zero Republican no votes, while only 19 of 201 Democrats voted yes against 175 no votes.

industries.note: The bill hands the company its approval by law, deeming every environmental and agency review complete and barring the EPA from interfering. The public benefit is indirect and marginal; the certainty accrues to the company.

The pipeline would open a direct route to Gulf Coast refineries for tar-sands crude, while the bill would block EPA restrictions and preempt normal review of the project's greenhouse and spill implications.

industries.industry: Pipeline construction contractors and industry workers
industries.note: Construction and related jobs are the bill's strongest public-facing benefit, and the bill's findings cite them. This gain runs alongside ordinary workers' interests even as the environmental cost falls on others.

industries.industry: Oil and gas pipeline industry generally
industries.note: Approving a pipeline by statute - rather than by permit - sets a template for congressional shortcutting of environmental review that other projects could invoke.
